body: Edit Operations & Edit Scripts: Insertion, Deletion, Substitution Edit operations are elementary transformations used to describe how one sequence can be changed into another. In standard Levenshtein distance, the permitted edit operations are: insertion, deletion, substitution. An edit script is an ordered sequence of these operations. The minimum cost of any valid script transforming the source sequence into the target sequence defines the Levenshtein distance. source sequence ↓ edit operations ↓ target sequence minimum valid script cost = Levenshtein distance The operation model becomes meaningful only after the sequence representation has been defined. One edit can act on bytes, Unicode code points, grapheme clusters, words, phonemes, biological symbols, or another application-defined unit. What Is an Edit Operation? Let Σ be an alphabet and Σ* the set of finite sequences over that alphabet. An edit operation makes a local change to a sequence. Operation Effect Example Standard Cost Insertion Add one sequence element ct → cat 1 Deletion Remove one sequence element cart → cat 1 Substitution Replace one sequence element cat → cut 1 A match is often represented in an alignment, but it is not normally counted as an edit because it does not change the sequence. match(a,a) cost = 0 insert(a) cost = 1 delete(a) cost = 1 substitute(a,b) cost = 1 Insertion An insertion adds one sequence element. ct ↓ insert a cat At the chosen representation level, insertion increases sequence length by one. If the sequence elements are words rather than characters: [the, cat] ↓ insert "black" [the, black, cat] the same abstract operation applies to a different kind of sequence. Deletion A deletion removes one sequence element. cart ↓ delete r cat Deletion decreases sequence length by one element at the selected representation layer. Substitution A substitution replaces one sequence element with another. cat ↓ substitute a → u cut A substitution preserves sequence length. Under standard unit-cost Levenshtein distance: substitution cost = 1 but generalized edit-distance models can assign another cost. Transformation Direction Matters Edit operations are interpreted relative to a transformation direction: source → target Consider: cat → cart From source to target, the change is an insertion of r . Reversing the direction: cart → cat changes the corresponding operation to deletion. Forward Operation Reverse Operation Insert a Delete a Delete a Insert a Substitute a → b Substitute b → a With symmetric unit costs, reversing an optimal script produces a reverse transformation with the same total cost. This contributes to the symmetry of standard Levenshtein distance. What Is an Edit Script? An edit script is an ordered sequence of permitted edit operations that transforms the source into the target. S = (o1, o2, ..., ok) Applying those operations sequentially gives: x ↓ o1 x1 ↓ o2 x2 ... ↓ ok y A script is valid only if applying all of its operations produces the exact target sequence. Example: Kitten to Sitting kitten ↓ substitute k → s sitten ↓ substitute e → i sittin ↓ insert g sitting This script contains two substitutions and one insertion. total cost = 1 + 1 + 1 = 3 Under standard unit-cost Levenshtein distance: ED("kitten", "sitting") = 3 Edit Script Cost Let c(o) denote the cost of operation o . The cost of an edit script S is: C(S) = Σ c(oi) Standard Levenshtein distance uses: c(insert) = 1 c(delete) = 1 c(substitute) = 1 The distance is the minimum script cost: d(x,y) = min C(S) over every valid script S such that S(x) = y Therefore: edit distance ≠ cost of any valid edit script edit distance = cost of a minimum-cost valid edit script A Valid Script Is Not Necessarily Optimal Consider: cat → cut One valid script is: cat ↓ delete a ct ↓ insert u cut Its total cost is two. A cheaper script is: cat ↓ substitute a → u cut whose cost is one. Both scripts are valid. Only the second is optimal under the standard unit-cost model. Substitution Versus Delete Plus Insert A substitution can always be represented as a deletion followed by an insertion. uav ↓ delete a uv ↓ insert b ubv Under the standard cost model: substitution = 1 deletion + insertion = 2 so direct substitution is cheaper. In a weighted model, if: c_substitute(a,b) ≥ c_delete(a) + c_insert(b) then using substitution provides no cost advantage over deleting a and inserting b . See Weighted Levenshtein Distance . Edit Scripts and Alignments An edit script can also be represented as an alignment. source: c a t | * | target: c u t Here: | = match * = substitution An insertion can be shown as a gap in the source: source: c - t target: c a t A deletion can be shown as a gap in the target: source: c a t target: c - t Alignment Column Interpretation a / a Match a / b Substitution - / b Insertion a / - Deletion Edit Operations in Dynamic Programming The Wagner–Fischer Algorithm computes the minimum cost of transforming prefixes of one sequence into prefixes of another. Define: D[i][j] as the minimum cost required to transform the first i source elements into the first j target elements. Under standard unit costs: D[i][j] = min( D[i-1][j] + 1, D[i][j-1] + 1, D[i-1][j-1] + cost ) cost = 0 if source[i-1] == target[j-1] 1 otherwise Transition Meaning D[i-1][j] → D[i][j] Deletion D[i][j-1] → D[i][j] Insertion D[i-1][j-1] → D[i][j] with unequal elements Substitution D[i-1][j-1] → D[i][j] with equal elements Match The visual direction of a matrix transition depends on which sequence is placed on each axis. The semantic operation should therefore be determined from the prefix-state definition rather than memorized from a particular diagram orientation. An Edit Script Is a Path Through Prefix States A complete edit script corresponds to a path from: (0,0) to: (m,n) in the dynamic-programming state space. Operation Source Elements Consumed Target Elements Consumed Deletion 1 0 Insertion 0 1 Substitution 1 1 Match 1 1 Recovering an Edit Script Once a complete dynamic-programming matrix has been computed, an optimal edit script can be recovered by backtracking from the final state. i = length(source) j = length(target) operations = [] while i > 0 or j > 0: if source and target elements match and diagonal predecessor is optimal: operations.append(MATCH) i -= 1 j -= 1 else if substitution predecessor is optimal: operations.append(SUBSTITUTE) i -= 1 j -= 1 else if deletion predecessor is optimal: operations.append(DELETE) i -= 1 else: operations.append(INSERT) j -= 1 reverse(operations) The script is reversed at the end because backtracking proceeds from target state toward the source state. The Optimal Edit Script May Not Be Unique The minimum numerical distance does not necessarily determine one unique script. Several predecessor states can satisfy: D[i][j] = D[predecessor] + operation cost with the same minimum total value. Therefore: unique distance ≠ necessarily unique optimal alignment This matters when software reports individual substitutions, deletions, or insertions rather than only the final distance. Tie-Breaking Changes the Reported Script When several optimal predecessors exist, an implementation can use a stable preference such as: match → substitution → deletion → insertion to produce deterministic output. This does not make the mathematical optimum unique. It simply selects one representative optimal path. A system reporting edit statistics should document its cost model, alignment rules, and tie-breaking policy. Edit Coordinates Must Be Defined Insertions and deletions shift later positions. abcdef ↓ delete b acdef A later operation described as occurring at “position 4” can refer to: the original source coordinates, the current intermediate sequence, the final target coordinates, alignment coordinates. APIs exposing edit scripts should define their coordinate system explicitly. Weighted Edit Operations Standard Levenshtein distance assigns unit costs, but application-specific models can define: c_insert(a) c_delete(a) c_substitute(a,b) For example, an OCR model could assign a lower substitution cost to character pairs that the recognizer frequently confuses. Operation Illustrative Cost Possible Interpretation substitute(m,n) 0.4 Frequent recognition confusion substitute(q,z) 1.5 Less plausible confusion delete(space) 0.3 Frequent segmentation error insert(character) 1.0 Default insertion The resulting algorithm minimizes total edit cost rather than simply counting operations. Asymmetric Costs Edit costs can be directional: c_substitute(a,b) = 0.4 c_substitute(b,a) = 0.8 Such models can be useful when one sequence represents the output of an error-generating process relative to another. But directional costs can produce: d(x,y) ≠ d(y,x) so the resulting function is no longer the ordinary symmetric Levenshtein metric. Zero-Cost Transformations and Preprocessing Some applications deliberately treat selected differences as irrelevant. One approach is to assign zero cost to a particular operation. Another is to transform the text before computing edit distance: raw text ↓ transformation T ↓ sequence representation ↓ edit distance If: x ≠ y but T(x) = T(y) then: ED(T(x), T(y)) = 0 This does not establish equality of the original strings. It establishes equality in the transformed comparison space. See Text Normalization and Transliteration . Transposition Is Not a Classical Levenshtein Operation Consider: hte the Two adjacent symbols have exchanged positions. Classical Levenshtein distance contains only: insertion deletion substitution so an adjacent transposition is not one primitive Levenshtein edit. Models that explicitly include transposition produce a different edit-distance model. See Damerau-Levenshtein Distance . The Operation Set Defines the Distance Model Allowed Operations Resulting Model Substitution only Related to Hamming distance on equal-length sequences Insertion + deletion Insert-delete distance related to longest common subsequence Insertion + deletion + substitution Standard Levenshtein distance Add adjacent transposition Damerau-style edit distance Symbol-dependent costs Weighted edit distance Gap-open + gap-extension costs Sequence-alignment models The phrase edit distance is therefore incomplete unless the sequence representation, operation set, and cost model are known. Insertion-Deletion Distance and Longest Common Subsequence When substitution is not available as a primitive operation, transformation can be performed using deletions and insertions. If L is a longest common subsequence of x and y , then under unit insertion and deletion costs: d_insdel(x,y) = |x| + |y| - 2|L| Symbols belonging to the common subsequence can remain unchanged. Other source elements are deleted, while missing target elements are inserted. What Exactly Is One Edit Unit? In software, the word character is often ambiguous. One edit can act on: bytes, encoding code units, Unicode code points, extended grapheme clusters, words or tokens, phonemes, DNA bases, other application-defined sequence elements. delete one byte ≠ delete one code point ≠ delete one grapheme cluster ≠ delete one word The abstract edit operation is the same, but its application meaning changes with the underlying sequence representation. Unicode Changes the Meaning of an Edit Consider the visible character: é Unicode can represent it as: U+00E9 or using a decomposed sequence: U+0065 + U+0301 A code-point-level edit model sees different sequence lengths in these two representations. Likewise, one user-perceived emoji or decorated text unit can contain multiple Unicode code points. Therefore: Unicode code point ≠ necessarily one user-perceived character See Unicode & Grapheme-Safe Levenshtein . Normalization Can Change the Edit Script Canonically equivalent Unicode text can produce different edit operations when compared before normalization. raw representation A vs raw representation B ↓ edit script 1 After canonical normalization: NFC(A) vs NFC(B) ↓ edit script 2 the two strings can become identical or require fewer operations. Therefore the edit script depends on the representation and transformation policy used before comparison. Unicode Text Transformations and Edit Operations A Unicode transformation can intentionally produce a new valid sequence. source Unicode text ↓ transformation T ↓ target Unicode text Edit distance can then describe the minimum sequence changes connecting the source representation and the result. source ↓ insert / delete / substitute ↓ result The transformation and edit distance are separate operations: transformation = produces the target representation edit distance = measures a minimum relationship between defined sequences This distinction applies to normalization, transliteration, case transformations, and other Unicode mappings. Continue with Unicode Text Transformations . Character-Level Versus Token-Level Edits Consider: the black cat the cat At word level: delete("black") is one edit. At character level, multiple characters and spacing must be removed. Sequence Unit Meaning of One Deletion Code point Remove one Unicode code point Grapheme cluster Remove one user-perceived text unit Word Remove one token Phoneme Remove one phonetic unit DNA base Remove one nucleotide symbol Edit Operations in Word Error Rate Automatic speech-recognition evaluation commonly applies insertion, deletion, and substitution to word sequences. S = substitutions D = deletions I = insertions N = reference words WER = (S + D + I) / N The edit operations resemble Levenshtein distance, but the sequence elements are words rather than characters and the final error statistic includes a task-specific normalization. See Word Error Rate and ASR Evaluation . Edit Operations in OCR Evaluation OCR systems can be evaluated through character-level or word-level insertions, deletions, and substitutions. Separating error types can reveal behavior hidden by a single aggregate edit distance. System Insertions Deletions Substitutions System A 10 8 82 System B 40 40 20 Two systems can therefore have the same total number of edit errors while producing very different error profiles. See OCR Evaluation and Post-Correction . Edit Operations in Biological Sequence Alignment Biological sequence analysis also uses insertion, deletion, and substitution concepts, but many alignment models use richer scoring systems. A gap of length five can be modeled as: one gap opening + four gap extensions rather than five independent unit-cost deletions. gap_cost(k) = gap_open + (k - 1) × gap_extend This is a different model from standard Levenshtein distance. See Sequence Alignment and Gap Models . Edit Scripts as Explanations A scalar distance answers: How much minimum editing separates the two sequences? An edit script additionally answers: Which permitted operations form one minimum-cost explanation of the difference? This makes edit scripts useful for: error analysis, visual diff interfaces, correction systems, sequence alignment, OCR analysis, ASR diagnostics, debugging. An Optimal Edit Script Is Not a Causal History Suppose an optimal script contains: substitute a → e This does not prove that a real-world process literally replaced an a with an e . It means only that substitution belongs to one minimum-cost mathematical transformation under the selected sequence representation and cost model. optimal edit script ≠ proven causal history The actual difference may have originated from typing behavior, OCR, speech recognition, data conversion, text normalization, or another process. The Conceptual Hierarchy source data ↓ optional transformation ↓ sequence representation ↓ allowed edit operations ↓ operation costs ↓ valid edit scripts ↓ minimum-cost script ↓ edit distance Changing the transformation, sequence representation, permitted operations, or operation costs can change both the edit script and the final distance. Key Distinctions Concept Meaning Edit operation One permitted sequence transformation step Match Zero-cost correspondence between equal sequence elements Edit script Ordered operations transforming source into target Valid script Any permitted script that reaches the target Optimal script A valid script with minimum total cost Edit distance Cost of an optimal script Alignment A positional representation of matches and edits Transformation A separate function that produces a new representation Summary Insertion, deletion, and substitution are the elementary operations underlying standard Levenshtein distance. An edit script combines these operations into a complete transformation from source to target, while Levenshtein distance is defined by the cost of a minimum-cost valid script. A minimum distance does not necessarily imply a unique alignment or edit script. Tie-breaking, coordinate systems, and representation choices matter whenever individual operations are interpreted. Weighted costs, transpositions, gap models, and other extensions create different edit-distance models. Unicode adds another essential requirement: one edit must be defined relative to a sequence representation. Bytes, code units, Unicode code points, grapheme clusters, and words are different edit units. Define the representation, define the permitted operations, define their costs, then interpret the edit script. body: Entity Resolution and Record Linkage Entity resolution and record linkage ask a deceptively difficult question: Do two records describe the same real-world entity? The records may contain names, addresses, dates, identifiers, telephone numbers, organizations, product attributes, or other fields. Values can be incomplete, misspelled, reformatted, transliterated, outdated, duplicated, or simply wrong. A typical pair might look like: RECORD A name: Jonathan A. Smith date_of_birth: 1984-07-16 address: 42 West Harrison Street postcode: 60605 RECORD B name: Jonathon Smith date_of_birth: 1984-07-16 address: 42 W Harrison St postcode: 60605 The names are not identical. The addresses are not identical. Yet the combined evidence may strongly suggest that the records refer to the same person. This is where string similarity, including Levenshtein distance , becomes useful—but only as one component of a larger inference problem. The central principle of this article is: String similarity is evidence about field values. It is not proof of entity identity. A reliable entity-resolution system therefore separates several problems: raw records ↓ standardization ↓ candidate generation ↓ field comparisons ↓ evidence combination ↓ pairwise decision ↓ optional global consistency ↓ entities / linked records Treating Levenshtein distance as the entire matching algorithm collapses these distinct stages into one number and usually produces poor decisions. Terminology: record linkage, deduplication, and entity resolution These terms overlap but are not always identical. Record linkage Record linkage traditionally refers to identifying records in different files that correspond to the same underlying entity. FILE A FILE B a₁ b₁ a₂ ↔ b₂ a₃ b₃ ... ... For example: hospital registry ↔ insurance database or: voter file ↔ survey respondents Deduplication Deduplication applies essentially the same reasoning within one collection: record 172 and record 9831 may describe the same entity Entity resolution Entity resolution is often used more broadly for the complete process of determining which observed records belong to which latent real-world entities. It may involve: cross-file linkage; within-file deduplication; multi-source integration; cluster formation; canonical entity construction. The terminology varies across statistics, databases, information retrieval, public health, knowledge graphs, and machine learning. What matters computationally is the structure of the matching problem. The latent-entity view Suppose observed records are: r₁, r₂, ..., rₙ but the real world contains latent entities: e₁, e₂, ..., eₖ with: k ≤ n Entity resolution seeks an assignment: zᵢ ∈ {1,...,k} where: zᵢ = j means that record rᵢ refers to entity eⱼ . Pairwise record linkage instead often focuses first on: Mᵢⱼ = 1 if records i and j match 0 otherwise The two formulations are related but not identical. Pairwise predictions can violate the global structure required by an entity partition. The fundamental distinction: similarity is not identity Consider: "John Smith" "Jon Smith" Their character strings are close. But millions of people can share those names. Now consider: "Aleksandr Sergeyevich Pushkin" "Alexander Pushkin" The strings may differ substantially, yet domain knowledge, transliteration, dates, locations, and other attributes could establish that both records describe the same person. Thus: small edit distance ⇏ same entity large edit distance ⇏ different entity This is a special case of the wider distinction developed in String Similarity vs Semantic Similarity . Entity resolution is an evidence-combination problem Suppose two person records provide: name date of birth street postcode email telephone Each field contributes a different kind of evidence. Observation Possible interpretation Same exact email Potentially very strong positive evidence Same surname Strength depends heavily on surname frequency Name edit distance = 1 Evidence of lexical similarity, not identity Different birth dates Could be strong negative evidence or one data-entry error Same postcode Weak or moderate evidence depending on population density Missing telephone Absence of evidence, not necessarily evidence of non-match The job of the linkage model is to combine these observations coherently. A complete linkage pipeline INPUT RECORDS │ ▼ ┌───────────────────────┐ │ parsing / cleaning │ │ standardization │ └───────────┬───────────┘ │ ▼ ┌───────────────────────┐ │ candidate generation │ │ blocking / indexing │ └───────────┬───────────┘ │ ▼ ┌───────────────────────┐ │ field comparison │ │ │ │ exact │ │ edit distance │ │ token similarity │ │ phonetic similarity │ │ numeric differences │ └───────────┬───────────┘ │ ▼ ┌───────────────────────┐ │ comparison vector │ └───────────┬───────────┘ │ ▼ ┌───────────────────────┐ │ evidence model │ │ probability / score │ └───────────┬───────────┘ │ ▼ ┌───────────────────────┐ │ match / non-match / │ │ review │ └───────────┬───────────┘ │ ▼ ┌───────────────────────┐ │ constraints / │ │ clustering │ └───────────┬───────────┘ │ ▼ ENTITIES Stage 1: standardization Raw field values often differ for reasons unrelated to identity. For example: "42 West Harrison Street" "42 W. Harrison St." "42 W HARRISON ST" A normalization pipeline might standardize: case; punctuation; whitespace; abbreviations; Unicode representation; date formats; telephone formats; known address conventions. But normalization changes the strings on which similarity is calculated. Therefore: normalize then compare is mathematically a different operation from: compare raw values The transformation policy must be explicit and reproducible. Multilingual names and transliteration require additional caution; these issues are treated more generally in Text Normalization and Transliteration . Over-normalization can destroy evidence Consider identifiers: AB-120 AB120 Removing punctuation may be harmless. But for another field: Unit 12 12 aggressive token deletion may remove meaningful structure. Normalization should therefore be field-specific rather than one universal text-cleaning function. Stage 2: candidate generation For two files containing: n and m records, exhaustive cross-file comparison requires: n × m candidate pairs. If: n = 10,000,000 m = 10,000,000 then: 10^14 possible pairs exist. Pairwise comparison alone is therefore not a scalable architecture. Blocking Blocking creates candidate subsets using inexpensive conditions. For example: compare records only if same birth year OR same postcode prefix OR same surname initial The objective is: retain nearly all true matches while eliminating the overwhelming majority of impossible pairs Blocking is a recall-sensitive filter Suppose two true records contain: postcode A: 60605 postcode B: 60606 because one postcode was entered incorrectly. If the only blocking rule is: postcode must match exactly the pair is never evaluated by the sophisticated linkage model. Its probability of matching downstream becomes irrelevant because: candidate recall = 0 for that pair This is analogous to exact candidate-generation requirements in large-scale edit-distance search. See Indexing and Filtering for Edit Distance . Multiple blocking rules A safer strategy frequently uses a union: C = C₁ ∪ C₂ ∪ C₃ ... where each Cᵢ comes from a different blocking condition. For example: RULE 1 same date of birth RULE 2 same postcode and similar surname RULE 3 same telephone suffix RULE 4 same rare surname and same city A true pair lost by one rule may survive another. Candidate generation and matching must be evaluated separately Suppose: true matches = 10,000 but blocking retains only: 9,500 true matches. Even a perfect classifier can recover at most: 95% of all true matches. Therefore: end-to-end recall ≤ blocking recall Stage 3: field comparison For each candidate pair: (a,b) the system constructs comparison features. Example: Field Record A Record B Comparison Name Jonathon Smith Jonathan Smith Edit distance 1 Date of birth 1984-07-16 1984-07-16 Exact agreement Street 42 W Harrison St 42 West Harrison Street Normalized similarity Postcode 60605 60605 Exact agreement The comparison vector might be represented as: γ(a,b) = ( name_similarity, dob_agreement, address_similarity, postcode_agreement ) Levenshtein distance as a field comparator For name fields: x = "Jonathon Smith" y = "Jonathan Smith" we may compute: d_L(x,y) = 1 This is useful information. But the number: 1 does not itself tell us: P( same person | d_L = 1 ) because that probability depends on: name frequency; other fields; the data-generating process; the candidate-generation mechanism; the population being linked. Distance can be discretized into comparison levels Instead of feeding raw distance directly into a probabilistic model, a system may use levels such as: level 0: exact agreement level 1: distance = 1 level 2: distance = 2 level 3: normalized similarity ≥ 0.8 level 4: otherwise disagree Each level can then receive its own statistical evidence weight. Length matters An edit distance of 1 has very different meaning for: "Li" → "Lu" than: "Alexandrovich" → "Alexandrovit" This is one reason normalized or length-stratified comparison levels may be useful. However, normalized edit similarity is an application-defined transformation, not the original Levenshtein metric. Weighted edit distance Some errors are more plausible than others. For example: 0 ↔ O 1 ↔ I rn ↔ m or neighboring keyboard characters may occur more frequently than arbitrary substitutions. A domain-specific comparator can use Weighted Levenshtein Distance . But learned or manually selected costs should not be interpreted directly as match probabilities unless a probabilistic model explicitly gives them that meaning. Different fields require different comparators A generic edit-distance comparator is inappropriate for every attribute. Field Possible comparator Name Edit distance, Jaro–Winkler, phonetic models Date of birth Exact match, component comparison, date difference Latitude/longitude Geographic distance Telephone Exact normalized number, suffix agreement Email Exact match, local/domain decomposition Address Structured address comparison Numeric amount Absolute or relative numeric difference The comparative behavior of Levenshtein, Jaro–Winkler, and phonetic methods is treated separately in Levenshtein vs Jaro–Winkler and Phonetic Matching . The Fellegi–Sunter framework The classical probabilistic foundation of record linkage was formalized by Ivan Fellegi and Alan Sunter in 1969. For a candidate pair, let: M = pair is a true match U = pair is a true non-match and let: γ be the observed comparison pattern. Define: m(γ) = P(γ | M) and: u(γ) = P(γ | U) The evidence supplied by comparison pattern γ can be expressed through the likelihood ratio: Λ(γ) = m(γ) / u(γ) or log weight: w(γ) = log( m(γ) / u(γ) ) A comparison pattern is strong positive evidence when it is: common among true matches but rare among non-matches Why rarity matters Suppose two records agree on surname: "Smith" and another pair agrees on: "Quenel" Exact agreement occurs in both cases. But if the first surname is extremely common and the second very rare, the evidential strength is not equal. Conceptually: rare agreement → large m/u ratio common agreement → smaller m/u ratio This is one of the central advantages of probabilistic linkage over a rule such as: +1 point for every agreeing field Field-level Fellegi–Sunter weights Suppose comparisons are divided into fields: γ = ( γ_name, γ_dob, γ_address, γ_postcode ) Under a conditional-independence approximation: P(γ | M) ≈ ∏ᵢ P(γᵢ | M) and: P(γ | U) ≈ ∏ᵢ P(γᵢ | U) Therefore: log P(γ | M) ───────── P(γ | U) ≈ Σᵢ log P(γᵢ | M) ────────── P(γᵢ | U) This gives additive comparison weights. Worked probabilistic example Suppose the estimated comparison probabilities are: Observation m u m/u Very similar name 0.80 0.02 40 Exact date of birth 0.95 0.003 316.7 Same postcode 0.70 0.04 17.5 The approximate combined Bayes factor under conditional independence is: 40 × 316.7 × 17.5 ≈ 221,690 That is far stronger evidence than simply saying: three fields look similar Prior probability matters Evidence must be interpreted relative to how likely two candidate records were to match before examining their comparison features. Let: π = P(M) Then prior odds are: π ───── 1 - π Posterior odds can be written conceptually as: posterior odds = prior odds × Bayes factor If two enormous files are cross-joined randomly, the prior probability that an arbitrary pair describes the same person may be extraordinarily small. Blocking changes the candidate population and therefore changes the effective prior match prevalence among evaluated pairs. Blocking and probability cannot be conceptually separated Suppose candidate generation only allows records sharing: birth year Then the evaluated pair population is no longer a random sample of all possible record pairs. The distribution: P(γ | U) among blocked non-matches can be very different from its distribution across arbitrary pairs. Model estimation and evaluation should reflect the actual candidate-generation process. The original three-way decision rule Fellegi and Sunter formulated decisions as: LINK POSSIBLE LINK NON-LINK rather than forcing every pair into a binary classification. Conceptually: high score ↓ MATCH intermediate score ↓ REVIEW / UNRESOLVED low score ↓ NON-MATCH This remains extremely useful in high-stakes applications. Clerical review is a decision region Human review should not be treated merely as: send random difficult cases to people Instead it can be modeled as a deliberate uncertainty region: score ≥ T_match → automatic match score ≤ T_nonmatch → automatic non-match otherwise → review Thresholds depend on the cost of: false links; missed links; human review. False matches and missed matches can have asymmetric costs For some tasks: false link ≫ missed link because incorrectly merging two people contaminates downstream records. In other tasks: missed link ≫ false link because failure to connect relevant observations has a higher operational cost. There is therefore no universal score threshold. Estimating m and u probabilities The probabilities: m = P(comparison | match) u = P(comparison | non-match) may be estimated using: labeled match/non-match pairs; high-confidence rules; mixture models; Expectation-Maximization; semi-supervised procedures; domain-specific estimation. Mixture-model view Candidate comparison vectors can be viewed as arising from a mixture: P(γ) = π P(γ | M) + (1-π) P(γ | U) where the true class: M or U is latent. Expectation-Maximization can estimate parameters in suitable probabilistic linkage models without complete labeled data. Conditional independence is convenient but often false Consider: city and postcode or: first name and sex These fields may be strongly dependent. If a model simply multiplies field likelihood ratios as though every comparison were conditionally independent, evidence can be double-counted. For example: same postcode + same city does not necessarily provide the same amount of independent evidence as: same postcode + same date of birth Dependence is one limitation of simple Fellegi–Sunter implementations Possible remedies include: joint comparison levels; interaction terms; logistic models; tree-based classifiers; Bayesian hierarchical models; neural comparison architectures. But greater model flexibility requires more data and creates additional calibration and interpretability problems. Missing values are not ordinary disagreement Suppose: record A telephone: +1 312 555 0184 record B telephone: missing Treating this as: telephone disagrees can generate unjustified negative evidence. A missing field may require a separate comparison level: missing / unavailable rather than agreement or disagreement. Missingness itself can be informative The situation becomes more complicated when: P(missing | M) ≠ P(missing | U) or when missingness depends on source, population, or entity characteristics. Thus: "ignore missing fields" is not universally statistically correct either. Frequency-sensitive comparisons A powerful refinement uses the frequency of the actual agreed value. Compare: surname = Smith with: surname = Zabriskie Even when both are exact agreements, the rare value can carry more discriminative evidence. This general principle extends to: names; addresses; postcodes; occupations; organization names. Value frequency and edit distance interact Suppose: "Smith" "Smth" and: "Quenel" "Quenell" both have small edit distance. Their match evidence can still differ substantially because: string similarity + population frequency + other attributes must be interpreted jointly. Deterministic linkage Not every linkage system is probabilistic. A deterministic rule might say: MATCH if: exact date of birth AND ( exact normalized surname OR name edit distance ≤ 1 ) AND same postcode Such systems can be: transparent; easy to deploy; easy to audit; effective in clean domains. But hard thresholds can behave discontinuously. Threshold cliff Suppose: accept name distance ≤ 2 Then: distance = 2 → acceptable distance = 3 → unacceptable even if every other field strongly agrees. A probabilistic model can instead let the name comparison contribute graded evidence. Supervised classification With labeled training pairs: (comparison_vector, match_label) entity resolution can be formulated as classification. Possible models include: logistic regression; random forests; gradient-boosted trees; support-vector machines; neural networks. The input can still contain classical field comparators such as Levenshtein distance. Feature example x(a,b) = [ name_edit_distance, normalized_name_similarity, dob_exact, postcode_exact, address_token_similarity, email_exact, telephone_suffix_match ] A classifier estimates: P( M = 1 | x(a,b) ) or another decision score. Labeled pair sampling is dangerous Suppose training non-matches are generated by selecting random record pairs. Most will be trivially different: different name different city different date of birth different address A model trained on these easy negatives may perform poorly on production candidates, because blocking deliberately selects difficult pairs that already share some attributes. Training and evaluation data should resemble the candidate distribution encountered at inference time. Pairwise probability is not the whole entity-resolution problem Suppose: P(A=B) = 0.95 P(B=C) = 0.95 P(A=C) = 0.05 Independent pair decisions can produce: A = B B = C A ≠ C which is incompatible with ordinary identity because equality is transitive. Identity is an equivalence relation For ordinary deduplication: A = A A = B ⇒ B = A A = B and B = C ⇒ A = C Pairwise classifiers do not automatically enforce this structure. Clustering One common approach constructs a graph: records = vertices likely matches = edges and derives entity clusters from the graph. But simple connected components can overmerge. Bridge-error problem Suppose: A ── B ── C ── D where only one weak incorrect edge: B ── C connects two genuinely different groups. Connected-components clustering merges: A B C D into one entity. Thus a single false-positive edge can create a much larger entity-level error. Bipartite linkage has structural constraints Suppose two files are known to contain at most one record per person. Then record: aᵢ should match at most one: bⱼ and vice versa. Independent pairwise probabilities can violate this one-to-one constraint. Global bipartite matching The pair scores can instead be considered jointly. Suppose: B1 B2 A1 0.91 0.89 A2 0.90 0.20 Greedily choosing the largest score first gives: A1 ↔ B1 and leaves: A2 ↔ B2 with a poor score. A global assignment may instead prefer: A1 ↔ B2 A2 ↔ B1 depending on the model and objective. Bayesian bipartite linkage Modern Bayesian formulations can treat the matching structure itself as the parameter of interest rather than assuming independent pair statuses. This makes it possible to represent: one-to-one matching constraints; posterior uncertainty; unresolved matches; different loss functions for final decisions. Mauricio Sadinle's Bayesian bipartite framework is an important example of this approach. Uncertainty should survive the linkage pipeline A common anti-pattern is: probabilistic linkage ↓ hard matched table ↓ pretend linkage was perfect ↓ downstream statistical analysis If linkage errors are non-negligible, downstream estimates can be biased. In statistical applications it can be important to propagate: linkage uncertainty into: subsequent inference Entity resolution can be iterative Initial high-confidence links can improve later decisions. For example: high-confidence matches ↓ learn source-specific errors ↓ improve comparator parameters ↓ resolve harder pairs But self-training can also amplify mistakes. Error propagation Suppose an incorrect high-confidence match is accepted early. If its values are then used to: train error models; construct canonical entities; generate new blocking keys; infer household relationships; one pairwise mistake can affect many later decisions. Canonical records are a separate problem After several records have been assigned to one entity: { "Jon Smith", "Jonathan Smith", "Jonathan A Smith" } the system may need to create a canonical representation. Possible policies include: most recent value; most frequent value; trusted-source priority; probabilistic latent value; retain all observed variants. Entity resolution and canonicalization should not be conflated. Evaluation requires ground truth When true match labels are available, pairwise evaluation can use: TP = true matched pairs predicted match FP = non-matched pairs predicted match FN = true matched pairs missed TN = non-matched pairs rejected Precision precision = TP ─────── TP + FP answers: Of predicted matches, how many were correct? Recall recall = TP ─────── TP + FN answers: Of true matches, how many were recovered? F1 score F1 = 2 × precision × recall ────────────────────── precision + recall provides one balance between precision and recall. But F1 implicitly assigns a particular relative importance to the two error types and may not reflect operational cost. Evaluate blocking separately Let: T = all true matching pairs and: C = candidate pairs produced by blocking Then blocking recall is: |T ∩ C| ─────── |T| The reduction ratio can be measured against the full pair space. A useful blocking method seeks: very high recall and very large pair reduction Pairwise metrics are not sufficient for clustering A clustering system can produce excellent pairwise scores while still creating poor entity groups. Cluster-level diagnostics can include: entity-count error; cluster precision and recall; overmerge rate; undermerge rate; cluster-size distortion. Overmerging Overmerging occurs when records from different real entities are assigned to one entity. true: {A,B} {C,D} predicted: {A,B,C,D} Undermerging Undermerging occurs when records from one real entity remain split: true: {A,B,C,D} predicted: {A,B} {C,D} These errors have different consequences and should be reported separately. Ground truth is often imperfect Entity-resolution benchmarks frequently rely on labels produced by: manual review; existing identifiers; historical linkage systems; semi-automated labeling. Those labels can themselves contain errors. A reported: precision = 99.8% should therefore be interpreted relative to the quality and representativeness of the reference labels. Evaluation must be stratified Aggregate metrics can hide severe weaknesses. Useful strata include: common versus rare names; complete versus missing records; short versus long names; language or script; source system; geographic region; record age; amount of corruption. Why demographic and linguistic variation matters Different populations can have different: name-length distributions; surname frequencies; transliteration patterns; address structures; missing-data patterns; household naming conventions. A comparator or threshold calibrated on one population can perform differently on another. Identity signals are domain-specific For people: name birth date address telephone may be useful. For organizations: company name registration number address website industry may be relevant. For products: SKU manufacturer model number title dimensions may matter. The statistical structure of linkage changes with the entity type. Names and addresses deserve their own treatment Names, addresses, and places have complex error modes involving: abbreviations; token reordering; nicknames; transliteration; street conventions; geographic hierarchy. These issues are developed in Name, Address and Place Matching . Patient identity has stronger safety constraints In healthcare, a false merge can incorrectly combine medical histories, while a missed match can fragment one patient's record. The relative costs are therefore very different from ordinary marketing deduplication. See Patient Identity Matching . Privacy changes the matching architecture Sometimes two organizations need to identify common entities without revealing raw identifiers to each other. This creates the privacy-preserving record-linkage problem: Organization A has identifiers Organization B has identifiers but raw identifiers must not be exchanged Cryptographic, encoded, or privacy-enhancing comparison mechanisms create an additional trade-off between: linkage accuracy; information leakage; computational cost; attack resistance. See Privacy-Preserving Record Linkage . Common failure mode: one global Levenshtein threshold A naive system might define: same entity if Levenshtein(nameA,nameB) ≤ 2 This fails because: names are not unique identifiers; short and long names behave differently; different scripts and transliterations behave differently; other attributes are ignored; common names create large collision populations. Common failure mode: averaging unrelated similarities Suppose: name similarity = 0.9 address similarity = 0.8 birth-date similarity = 0 email similarity = 1.0 Computing: (0.9 + 0.8 + 0 + 1.0) / 4 = 0.675 has no probabilistic interpretation unless the aggregation rule has been justified. Different fields have different reliability and discriminative power. Common failure mode: exact equality is not always stronger than fuzzy agreement Exact agreement on: surname = Smith may be weaker evidence than near agreement on a rare full name combined with exact date of birth. Evidence strength depends on probability, not merely comparator category. Common failure mode: treating all disagreements equally These discrepancies are not equivalent: birth date differs by one transposed digit versus birth dates differ by twenty years Nor are: "Jonathan" "Jonathon" and: "Jonathan" "Mohammed" A useful comparison system preserves severity information. Common failure mode: ignoring field quality Suppose one source's postcode field is known to be: 99.9% accurate while another source's free-text address is: frequently stale Their disagreements should not automatically receive equal negative weight. Common failure mode: blocking on corrupted fields A sophisticated model cannot recover candidate pairs that blocking permanently removed. Blocking should therefore use: multiple keys; robust representations; high-recall rules; measured candidate recall. Common failure mode: treating pair predictions as independent entities Identity constraints can be violated if pair decisions are made independently. This is especially dangerous in deduplication and multi-source clustering. Common failure mode: using transitive closure blindly If: A ~ B B ~ C simple connected components imply: A ~ C even if: A and C have strong contradictory evidence Global entity construction needs stronger reasoning than graph connectivity alone. Common failure mode: assuming a high match score is calibrated probability A model score: 0.97 is not necessarily: 97% probability of a true match unless calibration has been validated. Common failure mode: evaluating only easy pairs If test non-matches are random cross-file pairs, the task can appear nearly perfect because most pairs are obviously unrelated. Evaluation should include the difficult candidate population produced by the actual blocking process. Common failure mode: leakage from identifiers Suppose ground truth was constructed using: email address and the model then uses that same email field as a feature. Measured performance may partially reflect the procedure used to define the labels rather than generalizable resolution ability. Common failure mode: silently changing preprocessing If production normalization changes from: NFC to: NFKC + case folding comparison distributions can change even though the probabilistic model parameters remain unchanged. Preprocessing versions should therefore be part of model versioning. Production architecture RAW SOURCES │ ▼ ┌─────────────────────┐ │ schema mapping │ │ parsing │ │ normalization │ └─────────┬───────────┘ │ ▼ ┌─────────────────────┐ │ candidate blocking │ │ / indexing │ └─────────┬───────────┘ │ ▼ ┌─────────────────────┐ │ comparison features │ │ │ │ exact │ │ edit-distance │ │ phonetic │ │ geographic │ │ numeric │ └─────────┬───────────┘ │ ▼ ┌─────────────────────┐ │ probabilistic or │ │ supervised model │ └─────────┬───────────┘ │ ┌─────────┴───────────┐ ▼ ▼ high confidence uncertain │ │ ▼ ▼ automatic decision review / defer │ │ └──────────┬──────────┘ ▼ ┌─────────────────────┐ │ structural │ │ constraints │ │ clustering │ └─────────┬───────────┘ │ ▼ ┌─────────────────────┐ │ resolved entities │ └─────────────────────┘ What should be logged? For every decision, a production system should ideally retain enough information to reconstruct: which blocking rules generated the pair; the normalized field values; comparison levels; model version; match score or probability; decision threshold; manual-review outcome; cluster operation. This makes later audit and error analysis possible. Model drift The distribution of records can change through: new sources; new countries; changes in data-entry software; new normalization procedures; population shifts; changes in identifier availability. Therefore: P(γ | M) and P(γ | U) may change over time. Linkage systems need monitoring, not one-time calibration. A useful diagnostic decomposition When an end-to-end match is wrong, classify the failure by stage: 1. parsing error 2. normalization error 3. blocking miss 4. comparator weakness 5. model error 6. threshold error 7. clustering / constraint error 8. bad ground truth Without this decomposition, every failure tends to be blamed on: "the similarity algorithm" even when Levenshtein distance was computed perfectly. Decision table Problem Appropriate response Small spelling error in name String comparator such as edit distance Common surname Use frequency-aware evidence Millions of records High-recall blocking/indexing Multiple noisy fields Evidence-combination model One-to-one cross-file matching Consider global bipartite constraints Multiple records per entity Entity-level clustering/model Ambiguous cases Review or unresolved state Privacy-sensitive linkage Privacy-preserving linkage architecture Different scripts/languages Representation and transliteration-aware processing Where Levenshtein distance belongs The most defensible role for Levenshtein distance in entity resolution is: one field-level comparator inside a larger evidence system For example: name comparison │ ├── exact equality ├── Levenshtein distance ├── Jaro-Winkler └── phonetic signal address comparison │ ├── structured tokens ├── postcode └── geographic evidence date comparison │ ├── exact date └── component-level error ↓ linkage model This architecture respects what edit distance actually measures: the cost of transforming one sequence representation into another. It does not ask edit distance to answer a fundamentally different question: Are these two records the same entity? The deeper statistical lesson Entity resolution is an inference problem under uncertainty. The observed data are imperfect manifestations of an underlying identity. REAL ENTITY │ ├── source A │ ↓ │ noisy record │ ├── source B │ ↓ │ noisy record │ └── source C ↓ noisy record The task is therefore not merely: measure similarity but: infer the latent entity that most plausibly explains the observed records Summary Entity resolution and record linkage identify records that correspond to the same underlying real-world entity despite missing values, formatting differences, typographical errors, stale attributes, duplicated records, and other forms of data corruption. Levenshtein distance can be valuable in this process, particularly for noisy textual fields such as names. But edit distance measures string transformation cost, not identity. A small character distance is only one piece of evidence and should normally be interpreted together with other fields. A robust linkage architecture begins with representation and standardization, followed by high-recall candidate generation. Blocking is essential at scale because exhaustive pair comparison grows quadratically or as the cross-product of the input files. Any true match removed during blocking cannot be recovered by later modeling. Candidate pairs are then converted into comparison vectors. Different attributes require different comparison functions: textual edit distance for some names, exact comparisons for identifiers, structured address comparators, numeric differences, geographic distance, date logic, and domain-specific methods. The classical Fellegi–Sunter framework treats these comparisons as statistical evidence. Agreement patterns common among true matches but rare among non-matches receive large positive evidence weights. Common agreements provide less evidence. This explains why exact agreement on a rare surname can be much more informative than exact agreement on a common one. Simple Fellegi–Sunter implementations often use conditional independence to combine field weights, but real record attributes can be correlated. City and postcode, for example, can contain overlapping evidence. Missingness, source-specific error, and blocking-induced candidate distributions also complicate probability estimation. Modern entity resolution extends beyond independent pair classification. Bipartite linkage can impose one-to-one constraints, Bayesian methods can quantify uncertainty over entire matchings, and multi-record entity resolution must ensure that final clusters obey coherent identity structure. Pairwise match quality and entity quality are not equivalent. A single false-positive edge can join two otherwise correct clusters, while missed edges can fragment one entity into several. Evaluation should therefore examine both pairwise errors and entity-level overmerging and undermerging. The most important implementation discipline is to preserve stage boundaries: representation → candidate generation → field comparison → evidence combination → decision → entity structure When these layers are kept separate, Levenshtein distance becomes a precise and useful component of entity resolution rather than an overloaded similarity score asked to infer identity by itself. Continue studying Name, Address and Place Matching — field-specific matching for names, addresses, geographic records, abbreviations, transliteration, and structured location evidence. Patient Identity Matching — entity resolution under healthcare-specific error costs and identity constraints. Privacy-Preserving Record Linkage — linking entities when raw identifying attributes cannot be directly shared. Weighted Levenshtein Distance — nonuniform edit costs for domain-specific textual errors. Levenshtein vs Jaro-Winkler and Phonetic Matching — choosing string comparators for different error distributions. String Similarity vs Semantic Similarity — why lexical resemblance and real-world equivalence are different relations. Indexing and Filtering for Edit Distance — candidate reduction and scalable similarity filtering. Text Normalization and Transliteration — representation choices that affect multilingual string comparison. References Ivan P. Fellegi and Alan B.
